name: Sprites (Fly.io)

modes.label: Sprite, billed on actual CPU time + actual memory while awake
modes.note: Every Sprite has 8 vCPU; CPU billed on cumulative cpu.stat CPU time, memory on actual usage (platform-managed, ~8 GB cap in practice). Hot storage $0.000683/GB-h on bytes written only while awake (extra key disk_gib_h_running). Warm (~30 s idle) and cold states bill no CPU/RAM/hot storage. Granularity: 'metered per hour of active use', exact rounding unpublished. Region not selectable. [basis verified 2026-09-28] fly.io/pricing: CPU "Cumulative CPU usage measured by cpu.stat" $0.07/CPU-hour; memory "Actual memory usage" $0.04375/GB-hour; "Sprites have three states: running (billed), warm (not billed), and cold (not billed)"; idle window ~30 s (docs.fly.io/sprites/concepts/lifecycle). No minimum/floor published. Whether page cache counts in "actual memory usage" is not stated (likely cgroup memory, which includes cache - unverified); "billed hourly" rounding unpublished.

evidence.quote: By default, a Sprite's outbound is unrestricted: it can resolve and reach any domain.
pulls in the common development domains, GitHub, npm, PyPI, Docker Hub, and the major AI APIs among them

knobs.label: Share of session the Sprite is awake (not warm/cold)
knobs.why: A Sprite goes warm ~30 s after last activity; warm and cold states bill no CPU, RAM or hot storage (cold storage continues). Anything that keeps it awake (open TCP connection to its URL, stdout output, a held Tasks API call) keeps RAM billing. Default 1 = awake the whole session.

caveats: Pricing section says 'No plans and no tiers' while the FAQ on the same page (and Fly's 2026-09-09 article) describe optional plans; Hero $100 is confirmed current. Other tier prices/allowances come from the 2026-01-16 community post; the 2026-01-22 release note listed a different set (Recruit free, Adventurer $20, Legend $200, Mythic $2,000).

Plan fee is NOT credit: it buys per-resource unit allowances (CPU-h, RAM GB-h, storage GB-month) that are not fungible (Fly staff post 2026-01-16: "Usage beyond included amounts is billed at standard usage-based rates"). Encoded as included_cpu_h / included_ram_gib_h / included_storage_gib_month on each plan with included_usd 0, so the engine (which only knows a fungible included_usd) never credits unused CPU hours against RAM overage; until the engine consumes the buckets, plans are never auto-picked over PAYG and the PAYG price is an upper bound for heavy users. Fly account credits cannot pay plan fees.

Storage: disk_gib_month 0.02 is COLD storage on all bytes written, billed for as long as kept (including while awake). HOT storage $0.000683/GB-h ($0.50/GB-mo) additionally bills on the awake working set (mode key disk_gib_h_running). Checkpoint storage not priced separately; snapshot_gib_month 0.02 assumes checkpoints are billed as cold storage (unverified).
Memory is billed on actual usage; the engine's ram_util drives the bill. RAM cap ~8 GB in practice (16 GB advertised, 'not available yet' per Jan 2026 support reply). max_ram_gib 8.
Fixed shape: 8 vCPU, 100 GB filesystem ceiling, one managed Ubuntu image (no custom image), no region selection, no public IPv4/SSH.

FUTURE TARIFF (not yet applied; today 2026-09-28): effective 2026-10-01 CPU $0.03825/CPU-h and memory $0.021875/GB-h (fly.io/pricing-update; vendor example 2 CPU + 4 GB for 720 h: $226.80 -> $118.08). Storage rates unchanged. Card keeps current $0.07 / $0.04375 until then; the dollar value of plan allowances will roughly halve too.
Rates history: 2025-12-30 RAM $0.011/GB-h and storage $0.10/GB-mo; current RAM $0.04375 (~4x higher; change date not found).
PAYG running-concurrency cap unpublished (concurrency null). Limits return errors, never extra charges.
No benchmark data in benchmarks.json (perf null); docs claim warm resume 100-500 ms, cold wake 1-2 s.

fleet.tiers: Official current FAQ confirms Hero 100 running plus 100 warm sprites/org, cold unlimited; higher plans raise ceilings. PAYG creates 10/min; Adventurer 60/min to Mythic 240/min.
fleet.notes: PAYG simultaneous-running default unpublished. Pricing says no plans/tiers elsewhere while FAQ describes optional plans; historic community ladders are not treated as verified current entitlements. 300/1,000 account entitlement/approval needs confirmation, not inferred from creation rate.

audit_2026_09_29.source: checked against the provider's live pricing and docs pages

snapshot_auto.quote: The VM is suspended with everything in memory frozen in place. Compute billing stops. The next request resumes it in 100–500ms, and processes pick up mid-thought, exactly where they were.
snapshot_auto.note: Trigger: ~30 s idle -> 'warm' (memory+processes frozen, automatic resume on request/exec). Longer idle -> 'cold' (memory dropped, disk only; processes restart, Services auto-restart). User cannot choose or observe warm vs cold. Separately the platform takes automatic background filesystem checkpoints ('auto-' IDs, pruned over time; docs.fly.io/sprites/concepts/checkpoints: "the platform creates its own in the background as you work"). Filesystem is also continuously synced to object storage.

snapshot_on_demand.quote: A checkpoint snapshots the writable filesystem overlay: everything you've added on top of the base image. It does not touch the base image itself, and it does not capture anything that only lives in memory.
snapshot_on_demand.note: Filesystem only, no memory. Via CLI (sprite checkpoint create), REST API (POST /v1/sprites/{name}/checkpoint) or from inside (sprite-env / /.sprite/api.sock). Copy-on-write, non-interrupting, sequential v0..vN with comments; last 5 mounted read-only at /.sprite/checkpoints/. Restore is in place only (destructive); the public API has no create-from-checkpoint. Release notes (2026-04-02) mention a 'Fork a Sprite' by timestamp for 'Admins' on the 'admin sprite page' - appears to be operator/admin tooling, not in the public API/CLI docs.

harness_api.note: Public API surface is sprites, checkpoints, exec, fs, policies, services, connectors - no endpoint to start/prompt/stream/resume an agent harness. Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex, Cursor are preinstalled (agent_harnesses) and Sprites act as a sandbox backend for third-party harnesses (Claude Managed Agents self-hosted environment, Cursor Cloud Agents, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK adapters, remote MCP server), but the harness is driven by those vendors' APIs, not a Sprites harness API. Tasks API (in-VM) only keeps the Sprite awake.

egress_allowlist.quote: Egress can be tightened with a **network policy**, a DNS-based allowlist that decides which domains a Sprite is allowed to reach. Applying one is opt-in and done from outside the Sprite.
egress_allowlist.note: Per-Sprite allow/deny domain rules incl. wildcards and a 'defaults' preset; raw IP connections blocked unless resolved from an allowed domain; private IPs always blocked; live reload drops existing connections; read-only inside the Sprite ("a Sprite can't rewrite its own egress rules"). No IP/CIDR rules in the NetworkPolicyRule schema (domain/action/include only). Default is unrestricted.

egress_http_rules.quote: The access policy can also restrict which provider paths a Sprite can reach through the connector.
egress_http_rules.note: Only for traffic sent through the Connectors gateway: per-connector allowed_endpoints / blocked_endpoints path patterns (exact or trailing-* prefix; block wins), API-only. No method/header rules and no HTTP-level rules for general (non-connector) egress, which is DNS-level only.

ingress_rules.quote: A Sprite URL is private by default. It's reachable only by members of your org, through the browser or with an org token
ingress_rules.note: url_settings.auth sprite|public, plus private_access admins|organization (API). URL routes to one chosen HTTP port (service --http-port); other ports only via authenticated 'sprite proxy' / WebSocket TCP proxy. No IP allowlists, no public IPv4, no raw TCP inbound.

secret_proxy.quote: **Custom API** is the fallback for anything without a dedicated connector: give it a base URL, a token, and where the token goes, and it wraps any token-authenticated HTTP API.
secret_proxy.note: Connectors: credential stored encrypted in the org, Sprite calls https://api.sprites.dev/v1/gateway/<provider>/<connection_id>/<path> with no Authorization header (identity from Fly request signature); "Sprites never see the token." Not transparent: the agent must call the gateway URL (preinstalled sprite-api-gateway skill for Claude Code/Cursor/Codex/Gemini). OAuth (GitHub), BYOK and managed (OpenRouter) credentials; deny-by-default per-Sprite access by name prefix/labels. Header/query/path token placement. HTTP only; no DB/SSH/git-protocol coverage documented.

volume_attach.quote: Every Sprite starts with 100 GB of storage. It does not autoscale yet, so plan around that ceiling.
volume_attach.note: Single fixed 100 GB ext4 filesystem per Sprite; no volume endpoints in the OpenAPI and no attach option on create. (Fly Machines have volumes, but not Sprites.)

volume_shared.quote: It is not an object-storage shim or a network filesystem.
volume_shared.note: Per-Sprite filesystem only; no shared volume or bucket mount documented (SSHFS from a laptop is DIY).

docker_inside.note: Not directly confirmed for Docker specifically. Reasoned from: a Sprite is a real Firecracker microVM with its own kernel and root access ('root': true on the card), a full ext4 filesystem, and 'Full Linux — install any tools' (contrasted with a 'Fixed container image' for serverless functions in the same comparison table). No doc states containers are blocked; the Privileges Policy API only lets you further *restrict* capabilities/devices, implying they're unrestricted (root, cgroups, overlayfs) by default.

nested_virt.quote: Compute jobs at Fly.io are virtualized using Firecracker, the virtualization engine developed at AWS as the engine for Lambda and Fargate.
nested_virt.note: Not explicitly stated either way. Firecracker microVMs do not pass /dev/kvm through to the guest by default, and no Sprites doc (quickstart, lifecycle, networking, privileges-policy API) mentions KVM, nested virtualization, or running VMs/emulators inside a Sprite. Treated as not offered by default; derived from the Firecracker architecture, not a direct statement.

browser.quote: Sprites are persistent, hardware-isolated Linux environments for running arbitrary code. It's like having a small, stateful computer you can spin up on demand.
browser.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. Sprites is a general-purpose persistent Linux sandbox (AI code execution, dev environments, CI/CD); no managed/preinstalled browser or browser-automation product is documented anywhere in the Sprites docs, quickstart, or integrations pages.

anti_bot.quote: Sprites are persistent, hardware-isolated Linux environments for running arbitrary code.
anti_bot.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. Sprites has no browser product at all, so stealth/anti-fingerprinting against bot detection does not apply.

captcha_solving.quote: Sprites are persistent, hardware-isolated Linux environments for running arbitrary code.
captcha_solving.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. No CAPTCHA-solving capability is documented; Sprites is a generic compute sandbox, not a browser/scraping product.

live_resize.quote: You don't set or resize these yourself. The vCPU count and the storage ceiling are fixed; memory is handled automatically.
live_resize.note: vCPU (8) and disk (100 GB) are fixed and not user-resizable; memory autoscales automatically under platform control, not via a user-triggered live-resize API/CLI call.

own_agent_api.quote: Sprites are persistent, hardware-isolated Linux environments for running arbitrary code.
own_agent_api.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. Sprites is sandbox infrastructure that third-party coding/browser/computer-use agents (Claude Code, Claude Managed Agents, Cursor Cloud Agents, Codex, Gemini CLI) run inside; there is no first-party Fly/Sprites task agent, and the public API (openapi.json) has no endpoint to prompt/drive an own agent.

static_egress_ip.quote: Egress can be tightened with a network policy, a DNS-based allowlist that decides which domains a Sprite is allowed to reach.
static_egress_ip.note: Egress control is domain/DNS-based, not IP-based, and no fixed/static outbound IP is documented or offered anywhere in the Sprites docs (unlike, e.g., a dedicated public IPv4 which the card already marks false/unavailable).

sso.quote: Fly.io supports Google and GitHub as Identity Providers, and you can use one or both. ... You can, and usually should, require members of your organizations to use SSO.
sso.note: Org-level SSO via Google (OIDC) or GitHub, configured under org Settings > Single Sign On; applies to the Fly.io organization that owns and manages Sprites. Not SAML-based; Google/GitHub OIDC/OAuth only.

eu_data_residency.quote: You don't set or resize these yourself. The vCPU count and the storage ceiling are fixed; memory is handled automatically.
eu_data_residency.note: Region is not mentioned or selectable anywhere in the Sprites docs (quickstart, lifecycle, networking, index, maintenance) or on fly.io/sprites, unlike Fly Machines which documents an explicit multi-region list (docs.fly.io/reference/regions). No path to choose or guarantee an EU region for a Sprite was found; derived absence, not a direct statement.

max_session_h.quote: Sprites are persistent. Everything you leave is there when you come back, including the software. Long-living Sprites still need regular updates.
max_session_h.note: No documented maximum duration for a running/active session; Sprites are designed to be long-lived and are only paused by idle detection (~30 s to warm), not by an elapsed-time cap. No forced stop-after-N-hours is mentioned in lifecycle, quickstart, or the plans/pricing docs.

fork.quote: Restoring replaces the writable overlay with the saved state and restarts the environment. The base image is untouched.
fork.note: Restore is in-place/destructive on the same Sprite, not a clone into a new Sprite; the public API/CLI (checkpoints, exec, fs, policies, services, connectors per openapi.json) has no create-Sprite-from-checkpoint or clone endpoint. A 2026-04-02 release note mentions a 'Fork a Sprite' feature on an admin sprite page for 'Admins', but that's operator tooling absent from the public docs/API, not a customer-facing fork.

fork_running.note: No fork capability exists in the public API at all (see fork), so cloning a running Sprite without stopping it is a fortiori unavailable.

memory_snapshot_fork.quote: It does not touch the base image itself, and it does not capture anything that only lives in memory.
memory_snapshot_fork.note: Checkpoints (the only snapshot mechanism) are filesystem-only, not memory; combined with no fork capability at all, a memory-preserving fork is unavailable.

ssh.quote: Sprites don't expose SSH directly—you'll need to install an SSH server on your Sprite and tunnel the connection through `sprite proxy`.
ssh.note: No native SSH access; only a DIY workaround (install sshd yourself, tunnel via `sprite proxy -W :22`). `sprite console` is offered as the SSH-like interactive shell instead.

desktop.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. Sprites are headless Linux compute for coding agents (exec/console/fs/services); no VNC/RDP/stream desktop is documented anywhere in the Sprites docs or API.

computer_use.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. No desktop exists to drive by screenshots/clicks, and no such API appears in the Sprites OpenAPI or docs.

custom_image.quote: A checkpoint snapshots the writable filesystem overlay: everything you've added on top of the base image. It does not touch the base image itself
custom_image.note: Every Sprite starts from one fixed managed base image; you can only customize the writable overlay on top of it (and checkpoint that), not swap in your own base image at create time. No create-from-custom-image option in the API/CLI docs.

image_oci.quote: A checkpoint snapshots the writable filesystem overlay: everything you've added on top of the base image. It does not touch the base image itself
image_oci.note: Same fixed-base-image constraint as custom_image; no Docker/OCI image import for creating a Sprite is documented (Fly's separate Machines product supports OCI images, but Sprites does not).

volumes.quote: Every Sprite starts with 100 GB of storage. It does not autoscale yet, so plan around that ceiling.
volumes.note: Single fixed ext4 filesystem per Sprite backed by hot NVMe + durable object storage; no separate attachable volume resource or endpoint exists for Sprites (unlike Fly Machines, which does have fly volumes).

public_ipv4.quote: Every Sprite has one at `https://<name>-<org>.sprites.app/` (the org ID is a short generated identifier...), and it routes HTTPS to the Sprite's HTTP service.
public_ipv4.note: Inbound is exclusively via the HTTPS Sprite URL or the local `sprite proxy` tunnel; no per-Sprite public IPv4 address is issued or documented.

gpu.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. Each Sprite is a fixed 8 vCPU / platform-managed-RAM shape (docs.fly.io/sprites/concepts/lifecycle); no GPU option is mentioned anywhere in the Sprites docs, pricing, or FAQ (GPUs exist on Fly's separate Machines product, not Sprites).

windows.note: The 'macOS / Linux / Windows' toggle on the marketing page selects the *local* OS for installing the Sprites CLI, not the sandbox OS; the product itself is explicitly Linux-only compute.

macos.note: Same as windows: macOS only appears as a client-OS tab for the CLI installer, not as a sandbox guest OS. Product is Linux-only.

arm64.quote: Each Sprite runs with: 8 vCPUs, Memory the platform manages for you..., 100 GB of storage. You don't set or resize these yourself.
arm64.note: Fixed, unconfigurable resource shape with no architecture choice offered anywhere in the docs/pricing; no arm64 option is mentioned.

self_host.quote: Full Linux computers designed for agents instead of people.
self_host.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. Sprites is a hosted Fly.io service (billed per CPU/RAM/storage-hour on Fly's own infrastructure); no self-hosted/on-prem distribution is documented.

byoc.quote: Full Linux computers designed for agents instead of people.
byoc.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. No option to deploy the Sprites control plane into a customer's own cloud account is documented anywhere.

open_source.quote: Full Linux computers designed for agents instead of people.
open_source.note: Sprites is a proprietary hosted product on Fly.io's infrastructure; no OSI-licensed core-product repo is published (Fly does open-source some client tooling like flyctl, but not the Sprites runtime/service itself).

private_network.quote: By default, a Sprite's outbound is unrestricted... Egress can be tightened with a network policy, a DNS-based allowlist... Private IPs are always blocked, so a Sprite can't reach into private network ranges.
private_network.note: Networking model is public-internet egress (optionally allowlisted) plus a private-by-default HTTPS URL / local proxy for inbound; there is no VPC/private-network peering or Sprite-to-Sprite private networking documented, and private IP ranges are explicitly always blocked outbound.

egress_ip_type.quote: By default, a Sprite's outbound is unrestricted: it can resolve and reach any domain. Egress can be tightened with a network policy, a DNS-based allowlist that decides which domains a Sprite is allowed to reach.
egress_ip_type.note: derived: Sprites run as Firecracker microVMs on Fly.io's own datacenter infrastructure (docs.fly.io/security/security-at-fly-io); outbound traffic leaves through Fly's shared datacenter network, not a residential or mobile IP pool. No dedicated/static outbound IP is offered (static_egress_ip=false, public_ipv4=false), and no residential/mobile IP product is documented anywhere in the Sprites docs, so egress is ordinary shared datacenter IP space.

usage_api.quote: You can view and download invoices from the Billing section of your dashboard for each organization. ...To download a past invoice, click View for the relevant cycle. You'll be sent to the Stripe billing portal.
usage_api.note: granularity: account-only; cost: no; Billing data is accessible only via web dashboard and Stripe portal invoices. Metrics API (prometheus) provides live monitoring data (CPU/memory graphs) but no billable usage. No REST API, SDK call, or CLI command for per-Sprite/Machine billable usage breakdown or cost queries.

locations_quote: You don't set or resize these yourself. The vCPU count and the storage ceiling are fixed; memory is handled automatically.
